research_notes: From the 1981 album Sözüm Meclisten Dışarı (Türküola), with Kurtalan Ekspres. Music by bassist Ahmet Güvenç, lyrics by Manço; a requiem for his grandmother Nimet Manço (nicknamed Gülpembe). Year 1981 is the album release year.

title_english: Nassam Alayna al-Hawa (A Breeze Blew Upon Us)
research_notes: Written and composed by the Rahbani brothers for Fairuz. Arabic Wikipedia dates the release to 1967 and the film Bint al-Haris (بنت الحارس) to 1967 (Sout el-Sharq). Al-Bustan Seeds project page dates the film 1968; year 1967 follows the Arabic Wikipedia / original vinyl cited there. Filed here rather than in film_tv because it functions as a standalone Lebanese popular song; the film is noted in secondary_associations.

artist: Georgian State Merited Ensemble of Folk Song and Dance (Anzor Kavsadze)
research_notes: Kakhetian three-part polyphonic song dramatising preparations for battle. Cited by UNESCO (proclaimed 2001, inscribed 2008) as a prime example of Georgian polyphony. Voyager Golden Record includes a 2:21 performance by the Georgian State Merited Ensemble of Folk Song and Dance under Anzor Kavsadze (Voyager 2 launched 20 August 1977). Year left empty (traditional). Reference artist is the Voyager/UNESCO-cited ensemble, not a composer.

original_format: Vocal with piano or folk accompaniment
research_notes: Love poem written 1895 by Akaki Tsereteli; music composed the same year by his relative Varinka Tsereteli at his request (English Wikipedia). Widely known in the Soviet Union; translated into many languages. Only one page consulted. Year 1895 is the poem and (per that page) music year. Genre filed as romance because of its art-song/estrada life, not as Georgian folk polyphony.

Also known as Kâtibim. English Wikipedia calls it a Turkish folk song, an Istanbul türkü, about a clerk on the way to Üsküdar, and says many songs outside Turkey use the same melody with competing origin claims. German Wikipedia treats an Istanbul origin in the 19th century as possible, not proven, and notes a 1902 recording by Felix von Luschan. Sazname states that the Turkish-text version is an anonymous Istanbul türkü with no known poet or composer, and that the melody is shared across the late Ottoman and Balkan repertoire. English Wikipedia names Safiye Ayla's 1949 recording as a notable one. Year is empty because no consulted source fixes a composition date. Eartha Kitt's 1953 Uska Dara is a later American adaptation and is not given a separate record.

Persian tasnif. Persian Wikipedia: music by Morteza Neydavoud, poem by Mohammad-Taqi Bahar (Malek al-Sho'ara). First performance at a celebration for the newspaper Nahid on 7 Tir 1306 of the Iranian solar calendar; the first commercial recording, that autumn, was Moluk Zarabi with Neydavoud on tar, on Polyphon. The mode is mahur, with a passage into shur. English Wikipedia calls it an early-20th-century tasnif and a protest song. Sazgah likewise names Bahar, Neydavoud, mahur, and the 1306 Zarabi recording with tar and with violin by Musa Neydavoud. The Gregorian year is not printed in these sources, so the year field is empty; the Iranian year 1306 is the date they give. Later performances by Mohammad-Reza Shajarian are covers of this tasnif.

secondary_associations: Six-Day War | Basque lullaby Pello Joxepe
research_notes: Written by Naomi Shemer for the Israeli Song Festival. English Wikipedia: commissioned by Jerusalem mayor Teddy Kollek as a non-competitive piece; first sung by Shuli Natan on 15 May 1967. After the capture of the Old City on 7 June 1967 she added a verse. The National Library of Israel blog quotes Shemer: Gil Aldema of Kol Israel asked her, at Teddy Kollek's request, in the winter of 1967, and she chose 20-year-old soldier-teacher Shuli Natan, who sang it with her guitar. English Wikipedia also says Shemer later acknowledged that the melody draws on the Basque lullaby Pello Joxepe, which she had heard from Paco Ibáñez, and that Ibáñez did not treat this as plagiarism. Guitar is from Shemer's own account on the NLI blog, not from a session sheet.

title_english: I am on a long narrow road
research_notes: Turkish Wikipedia's song page: written in 1966 by the Turkish folk poet Âşık Veysel (Veysel Şatıroğlu), a türkü in the hüseynî makam in 4/4, from the Şarkışla area of Sivas, registered in the TRT Turkish folk archive as repertoire number 2973. His biography page names the bağlama as his instrument and lists this song among his works. English Wikipedia calls it one of his best-known songs. The 1966 date comes from the Turkish song page only. Bağlama is taken from the biography's description of his instrument, not from a session log for this recording.

Title song of Sezen Aksu's album Gülümse. The Turkish song page says the words come from Kemal Burkay's poem Hadi Gülümse, the music is by Arto Tunçboyacıyan, and the arrangement is by Onno Tunç. The English album page's track list agrees: writer Kemal Burkay, composer Arto Tunçboyacıyan, length 5:03. Turkish Wikipedia dates the album to 29 May 1991 (Coşkun Plak) and the song's video to 9 August 1991; English Wikipedia dates the album release to 16 July 1991. Year 1991 is agreed. This record is the song, not the whole album.

Lead track of Tarkan's album Ölürüm Sana, released 15 July 1997 on İstanbul Plak; the video is dated 10 July 1997 on the Turkish song page. That page and MusicBrainz credit the lyric to Sezen Aksu and the music to Aksu, Tarkan and Ozan Çolakoğlu, arranged by Çolakoğlu. English Wikipedia says the music was credited to Tarkan and that he later said, in a 2006 interview, this had been done without Aksu's consent. The three-way music credit follows the Turkish article and MusicBrainz; the dispute is noted rather than resolved. Also known abroad as Kiss Kiss.

Persian Wikipedia: folk-rock song by Kourosh Yaghmaei, lyric by his university classmate Mehdi Akhavan Langarudi. The song page says it was recorded in the Iranian year 1350 and released on his first album. The album page says the album Gol-e yakh was recorded on 30 Mehr 1352 at Studio Pop and released in 1352 by Beethoven (Iran), and lists the track at 5:14 with Yaghmaei as composer and arranger. Because 1350 and 1352 are both given, and neither page prints a Gregorian year, the year field is empty. A later performance associated with the Googoosh academy is a cover, not this record.

original_format: Vocal with traditional and electronic instruments
research_notes: Hebrew poem by the 17th-century rabbi Shalom Shabazi, opening 'even if the gates of the generous are locked, the gates of heaven are not locked'. English Wikipedia: Ofra Haza sang it on television in 1978 with the Shechunat Hatikva Workshop Theatre; the recording on Yemenite Songs (also Fifty Gates of Wisdom) is from 1984, length 5:18, and a dance remix produced by Izhar Ashdot was released in 1988. The album page says Yemenite Songs was released in Israel in November 1984, recorded August–September 1984, produced by Bezalel Aloni and Benny Nagari, mixing traditional percussion with drum machines and synthesizers. Her official site credits lyrics and music to Shabazi and the arrangement to Benni Nagari. Year 1984 is the album recording. The 1988 single is a remix of that recording.

English Wikipedia and the National Library of Israel exhibition agree that the song was made in Jerusalem in 1918, for the Balfour Declaration and Allenby's capture of the city, by adapting a Hasidic nigun and adding Hebrew words, and that Abraham Zevi Idelsohn intended it for a choir. The NLI says he had transcribed the Sadigura Hasidic melody in 1915 and published it in his Thesaurus. Wikipedia also records a competing claim that his student Moshe Nathanson wrote the words; Idelsohn's own English Wikipedia page still credits Nathanson with the lyric. The Hebrew University Jewish Music Research Centre says the first commercial recording, by Idelsohn's choir, was issued in 1922 on the Polyphon/Polydor Hebrew Palestinian folksong series. Year 1918 follows the composition date given by Wikipedia and the NLI. The lyric credit is disputed, so the record is only partially verified. Harry Belafonte's 1959 Carnegie Hall performance is a later cover. The song predates the State of Israel; it is filed under Israel as Israeli folk, with Jerusalem in 1918 noted.

secondary_associations: Beirut | Concierto de Aranjuez | Ziad Rahbani
research_notes: English Wikipedia names Li Beirut among Fairuz's civil-war songs. Antiwar Songs credits the lyric to the Lebanese poet Joseph Harb, the melody to Joaquín Rodrigo's Concierto de Aranjuez, and the adaptation to Ziad Rahbani, and says Fairuz recorded it on the 1987 album Maarifti Feek. Voice of Lebanon News says the singer Osama Hallaq performed it first, with Ziad Rahbani at the piano, broadcast in 1983, before Fairuz's album version. Year 1987 is Fairuz's album; 1983 is the earlier radio performance. Piano is documented for the 1983 Hallaq performance, not as a published solo edition. This is not a film song. Rodrigo's concerto itself is Western art music and is not duplicated here.

One melody sung with different words in Azerbaijan (Sarı gəlin), Armenia (Sari aghjik), eastern Turkey (also Erzurum Çarşı Pazar) and Iran. English Wikipedia says the origin is contested and that all versions use the Bayati mode. Azerbaijani and Turkish Wikipedia say Asaf Zeynallı wrote it down and arranged it for piano in the early 1930s. That is why a piano version is marked Yes: it is his early-1930s piano arrangement, not a later pedagogical edition. No composition year is known. Filed once, under Azerbaijan, because the Azerbaijani article and the English article's Azerbaijani section document the text and Zeynallı's notation; Armenia, Turkey, Iran and Georgia stay in secondary associations. Alim Qasimov's 2012 Eurovision interval performance is a later use.
